answer: The comparator chosen in an economic evaluation determines what cost-effectiveness means. Comparing a program to doing nothing answers only whether it works at all, but real resource-allocation decisions compare a program to the next best alternative that competes for the same budget. With a fixed budget, funding one program means forgoing another, so the relevant comparator is the alternative actually displaced, not a baseline of zero. Choosing the wrong comparator can make a program look favorable when, against its true alternative, another option dominates by producing more health for the same money.

faqs.q: What is the right comparator in a cost-effectiveness analysis?
faqs.a: The right comparator is the next best alternative that competes for the same resources. When deciding between two programs on one budget, each is the relevant comparator for the other, not a baseline of doing nothing.

faqs.q: When is comparing to nothing actually appropriate?
faqs.a: Comparing to nothing fits proof-of-concept or clinical-efficacy questions, where no alternative exists or the goal is testing a biological effect rather than allocating a fixed budget across competing programs.

faqs.q: What does dominance mean in comparing programs?
faqs.a: One program dominates another when it produces more health for the same or lower cost. A dominated program should not be funded, since reallocating its budget to the dominant option yields more health.
